say.text: Exam stem: which groin hernia is most likely to strangulate?
Go with your first instinct.

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, because indirect is the commonest inguinal hernia. But 'groin' also takes in the femoral canal, and femoral carries the highest strangulation risk of the groin hernias.
Indirect is more dangerous than direct, but it is not the groin answer.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the scope word first: 'groin' widens the list to femoral.

say.text: Tempting, because a direct hernia is the bulging, visible one. But a direct hernia is the classic answer for 'rarely strangulates', because its neck is wide.
Size is not the risk; the neck is.
Ask what the word 'groin' adds to 'inguinal'. Then ask which site sits below the inguinal ligament.
Yes. Femoral hernia has the highest strangulation risk of the groin hernias, so 'groin' points to it.
Which statement about hernias in women is correct?

choices.label: Femoral is relatively commoner in women, but indirect still ranks first
Femoral outnumbers every inguinal type in women, so it ranks first
Direct inguinal hernia is the commonest type in women overall
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, because femoral really is relatively more common in women. But 'relatively' compares the sexes; it is not a ranking within women, and femoral does not outnumber indirect inguinal.
Tempting, because the question is about women, so a female-only list feels like the right frame. But the ranking in women is led by indirect inguinal, the same as overall.
Read the qualifier in the stem. Is the claim about a comparison between sexes, or about a ranking within women?
Yes. Femoral is relatively more common in women, yet indirect inguinal is still the most common hernia in women.
Between the two inguinal hernias, which is more likely to strangulate?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, because direct hernias look bigger and bulge more. But a bulge is not the risk: a direct hernia has a wide neck and is the classic 'rarely strangulates' type.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trust the neck, not the size of the swelling.

say.text: Tempting, because two sacs sound like double the danger. But a pantaloon hernia is still judged by its necks, and the indirect sac is the one with the narrow neck.
Think about the neck the contents pass through, not how big the swelling looks.
Yes. Indirect hernias are more liable to strangulate than direct ones, because their sac passes through a narrow deep ring.
Indirect hernias are more liable to strangulate. Why?

choices.label: A narrow neck at the deep ring constricts the contents
A wide neck lets more bowel slide into the sac
Its larger bulge compresses the blood vessels inside the sac
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, because more bowel in the sac sounds like more harm. But a wide neck is the direct hernia's feature, and it is the narrow neck that strangles the contents.
Tempting, because a large bulge looks like it squeezes things. But the danger starts at the neck, where venous return is cut first, not at the outer bulge.
Look at the structure the contents must pass through, and ask what it does when the contents swell.
Yes. A narrow neck grips the contents: venous return is obstructed first, then arterial supply fails, and the bowel gangrenes.
Same question, two wordings. Which pairing is right?
Option A: most likely to strangulate in a groin hernia. Option B: most likely to strangulate in an inguinal hernia.

choices.label: Femoral for groin, indirect for inguinal
Indirect for groin, femoral for inguinal
Direct for groin, indirect for inguinal
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, because you have just answered indirect, and it is easy to keep it. But 'groin' takes in femoral, the highest-risk groin hernia. Femoral is not an inguinal hernia, so it does not answer the inguinal wording.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so read the scope word first: groin includes femoral, inguinal does not.

say.text: Tempting, because direct is the bigger, more visible hernia. But direct is the one that rarely strangulates, so it cannot answer either wording.
Ask which of the two words lets you include the femoral canal.
Yes. 'Groin' takes in femoral, which carries the highest risk. 'Inguinal' keeps you to the two inguinal types, where indirect is higher.
Worked case first. A 66-year-old woman has a tense, tender groin lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. It cannot be pushed back, and she is vomiting.
The senior's plan: resuscitate, go straight to theatre, and avoid forceful reduction, because the bowel may already be dead.
A junior wrote this plan for the same woman.
1. Diagnose a strangulated femoral hernia. 2. Gentle, then firm, taxis under sedation. 3. If it fails, go to theatre.
Which step is the mistake?

choices.label: Diagnosing it as a femoral hernia
Gentle, then firm, taxis under sedation
Going to theatre without a scan
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, if you rank groin hernias by the inguinal list, where femoral looks rare. But femoral is the groin hernia with the highest strangulation risk, so the diagnosis is right.
Tempting, because a scan before a big operation feels careful. But a tense, tender, irreducible swelling with toxicity is a clinical diagnosis, and a scan would only delay theatre.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so notice the step that is actually dangerous: the taxis, not the lack of a scan.

say.text: Look at step 2. Ask what it does to a loop of bowel that may already be dead.
Yes. The taxis is the mistake: forcing a strangulated lump back can return gangrenous bowel or reduce the whole sac en masse.
Why is that step dangerous when strangulation is suspected?

choices.label: It can push gangrenous bowel back or cause reduction en masse
It can make the hernia irreducible and delay the repair
Once analgesia is given, taxis becomes safe to try
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, because reduction is the goal in every hernia, so taxis looks like progress. But in strangulation the reduction is the danger: a dead loop goes back with the living bowel.
Tempting, because pain relief makes gentle handling feel safe. But analgesia changes comfort, not the blood supply of the bowel, so no drug makes taxis safe here.
Ask what is inside the sac, and whether it is still alive.
Yes. A strangulated loop may already be gangrenous. Pushing it back can return dead bowel to the abdomen, or reduce the sac and contents together with the constriction still present.
A man has groin pain, but no lump on examination. You suspect an occult hernia.
Which investigation do you order first?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, because CT looks like the most complete scan. But CT is kept for complicated or obscure presentations, not as the first test for an occult hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so match the test to the question: first test for occult, CT for complications.

say.text: Tempting, because it looks directly at the sac. But herniography is a historical test that has largely been replaced by cross-sectional imaging.
Ask which test is the first, widely available look at the groin for an occult hernia.
Yes. Ultrasonography is the first test for an occult hernia; MRI follows if the ultrasound is inconclusive.
A fit man has a visible, reducible groin swelling with an expansile cough impulse.
What is your next step?

choices.label: Ultrasound of the groin before surgery
CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, because a scan before a big operation feels careful. But imaging answers an occult or uncertain swelling; this one is clinically evident, so a scan only delays.
Tempting, because CT is the most thorough test. But CT is reserved for complicated presentations, not a reducible hernia with a clear cough impulse.
Ask whether the hernia is already evident on examination, or still in doubt.
Yes. A clinically evident hernia is a clinical diagnosis, so imaging adds nothing to the decision to repair.
A tense, tender, irreducible groin swelling, with vomiting, in a toxic patient.
What comes first?

choices.label: Resuscitate and take to emergency surgery
Gentle, then firm, manual reduction first
Ultrasound of the groin, then decide
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, because reducing is the habit for every groin lump. But with these signs, reduction can push dead bowel back or reduce the sac en masse, so the first move is resuscitation and operation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the reducible-hernia habit. Strangulation changes the first step.

say.text: Tempting, because a scan feels like the careful first step. But this swelling is clinically strangulated, so the scan delays theatre; imaging answers an occult lump, not a toxic patient.
Ask what this patient needs in the next minute, and whether the bowel can still be alive.
Yes. Resuscitation and emergency surgery come first, so that the bowel can be assessed for viability and resected if dead.
At surgery for a femoral hernia, the sac holds an inflamed appendix.
Which eponym fits?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, because both eponyms hold the appendix, so they feel interchangeable. But Amyand's is the appendix in an inguinal sac, and the site is what separates the two names.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so anchor each name to its site: inguinal for Amyand's, femoral for de Garengeot's.

say.text: Ask which groin site this sac lies in, and let that site choose the name.
Yes. De Garengeot's hernia is the appendix within a femoral sac.
Amyand's hernia is named for an appendix found in a hernia sac.
Which site is that sac in?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, because you remember the appendix and the femoral sac as one pair. But the femoral sac with an appendix is de Garengeot's; Amyand's sac is inguinal.
Think about which of the two groin sites lies above the inguinal ligament.
Yes. Amyand's hernia is the appendix within an inguinal hernia sac, so it lies in the inguinal canal.
Exam stem: the most common hernia in females.

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tempting, because femoral is the groin hernia that is relatively commoner in women. But relatively more common is not most common; indirect still leads.
Tempting, because a direct hernia is a common adult hernia. But it does not lead in women: indirect inguinal is still the most common hernia in women.
Check the qualifier: is the question asking which is most common, or which is relatively more common?
Yes. Indirect inguinal hernia is the most common hernia in women, even though femoral is relatively commoner in women than in men.
